nodes.name: Cation exchange at 570°C
nodes.procedure: The CFP loaded with ZnO NRs was placed in the centre of a tube furnace and nickel chloride (NiCl2) powder was placed 4 cm upstream from the tube centre. After the quartz tube was outgassed under vacuum, N2 gas with a flow rate of 50 s.c.c.m. was introduced into the system. The furnace was heated to and kept at 570 °C for 30 min, and then cooled down to room temperature. This produces NiO NRs with poor O-vacancies (NiO NRs-p-Ov).

nodes.characterization_summary: NiO NR preserves highly crystalline nature with lattice fringe spacing of 2.4 Å corresponding to (111) plane.
nodes.evidence_snippet: The transition electron microscopic (TEM) image (Fig. 2d) demonstrates that as-exchanged NiO NR preserves the highly crystalline nature of ZnO template after the cation exchange process, with a clearly identified lattice fringe space of 2.4 Å corresponding to the (111) plane of the cubic NiO (Fig. 2e).

nodes.characterization_summary: NRs consist of only Ni and O elements, without Zn signals, confirming complete transformation.
nodes.evidence_snippet: Notably, the element analysis indicates that as-exchanged NRs consist of only Ni and O elements, without any Zn signals, confirming the complete transformation of ZnO into NiO (Fig. 2f and Fig. S3).

nodes.characterization_summary: All peaks match typical crystalline structure of cubic NiO, without detectable ZnO peaks.
nodes.evidence_snippet: This is further verified by the X-ray diffraction (XRD) characterization that all the peaks of as-exchanged products well match those of the typical crystalline structure of cubic NiO (Fig. 2g), without detectable peaks from ZnO.

nodes.characterization_summary: O 1s spectrum shows peaks at 529.4 eV (lattice oxygen), 530.9 eV (defect sites with O-vacancies), and ~532.5 eV (surface-adsorbed water); relative O-vacancy amounts increase with exchange temperature.
nodes.evidence_snippet: In O 1s spectrum, three peaks can be clearly identified (Fig. 3a and Fig. S6). In detail, the peak at 529.4 eV (Peak I) is assigned to the lattice oxygen [24], whereas the peak at 530.9 eV (peak II) is attributed to a high number of defect sites with lower oxygen coordination [25], and the peak at ~532.5 eV (peak III) is associated with surface-adsorbed water molecules [25].

nodes.evidence_snippet: The calculated values for NiO NRs-p-Ov, NiO NRs-m-Ov, and NiO NRs-r-Ov are 5.43 × 10^20, 7.90 × 10^20 and 1.80 × 10^21 cm^-3, respectively, indicating the best electronic conductivity of NiO NRs-m-Ov.
